items.title: 5 Most Underrated Movies of 1997
items.summary: 1997 is the year that brought us modern-day classics like Titanic, Men in Black, and Princess Mononoke. Like any other year, there were inevitably some films that, in retrospect, may have been treated either too harshly or not given their due attention at all. Let’s take a look at some of the most underrated and overlooked movies of 1997. Funny Games 'Funny Games'Credit: The Criterion Collection Not to be confused with the 2007 English-language remake of the same name, and by the same director, Michael Haneke’s 1997 original Austrian film, Funny Games, is one of the more sadistic meta-horror thrillers of its time. The film is critically revered and well-known in many inner film circles, but this is one that, when I bring it up to many people I know who aren’t directly tied to film somehow, they usually wind up scratching their heads. Understandably, the film doesn’t give off the impression that it’s terribly accessible to an untrained eye. It’s subtitled, contains scenes of graphic, horrifying violence against the central family, and on top of that incorporates a chilling sense of meta commentary to the whole thing. The featured image above shows one of the intruders breaking the fourth wall in an extended, voyeuristic shot that is one of the most famous from the film. It’s certainly not a film for everyone, but if you’re looking to expand your taste a bit, look no further. Crash ‘Crash’Credit: New Line Cinema This one may seem like a bit of a cheat, since technically David Cronenberg’s Crash premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 1996; however, it was not distributed widely in the US or UK until Spring of 1997. A lot of this had to do with the extreme subject matter and sexual content of the film, which landed the film the infamous NC-17 rating in the United States, the first film to do so since Showgirls in 1995. items.title: The Uncanny Power of Famous Actors' Final On-Screen Lines
items.summary: I love movies so much, mostly because you never know what magic you're going to get on screen. From the real, accidental dolphins in The Odyssey to the shooting stars you can see in Jaws, when you run a camera, you never know what you're going to get. Sometimes, it's the final words of someone famous on screen. Whether by sheer coincidence or an intentional meta-narrative, legendary performers often have their final words to the public play out on screen. Today, I want to look at a few that I find to be quite powerful. Let's dive in. Actors' last scenes ever www.youtube.com 1. Robin Williams — Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb (2014) "Smile, my boy. It's sunrise." Damn, that made me cry. I loved Robin Williams so much. He was an inspiration to me and to many of my friends in comedy. Robin Williams brought immeasurable warmth to his performance as Teddy Roosevelt throughout the Night at the Museum trilogy that sort of made you believe he would be around forever. In his final live-action role, we hear these words before his character reverts to a wax figure as the morning light breaks over the museum. It's an awesome reminder to see the best in every situation and to look forward to new days. 2. Val Kilmer — Top Gun: Maverick (2022) "One last thing... Who's the better pilot? You or me?" Val Kilmer’s return as Tom "Iceman" Kazansky was one of the most emotional highlights of Top Gun: Maverick. I saw this movie on opening night, and you could hear people crying during this scene. And yes, one of them was me. The poignant connection of these two men with the meta-revelation of their roles was so special. This final humorous line breaks the tension of the scene and brings joy back ot he forefrotn. The brotherhood and ball-busting show that nothing changes, even as sickness takes everything else from us. 3. Oliver Reed — Gladiator (2000) "Shadows and dust."
